intro: Seven of the twelve trees on this page sit within a kilometre of Perugia's centre, which makes it one of the tighter walks on this site. Six are cedars and cedar relatives, planted through the nineteenth century as the city laid out its public gardens. The rest stand well outside that walk, on their own: two country oaks at Prepo, a downy oak up a hillside road, and a cypress in Ponte Felcino with the thickest trunk on this page.
meta_description: Twelve monumental trees in Perugia, most within a kilometre: cedars on the old fortress site, holm oaks that watched 1859, and Prepo's giant oaks.
question_meta: Perugia's oldest documented tree is the Palazzo Murena cedar, planted around 1861 in the university's cloister. Where it stands, plus eleven more.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Perugia that carries a date is the Cedar of Lebanon in the cloister of Palazzo Murena, planted around 1861 and so roughly 165 years old. It is free to walk in and see, in the courtyard of the university's rectorate in the historic centre. The holm oaks of the Giardini del Frontone are almost certainly older, since the gardens were laid out from 1707 and a local history piece describes them as already grown when papal troops sacked the city in 1859, but no source puts a number on them.
question_context: Perugia's trees are unusually well recorded for Italy, and the reason is that most of them stand on ground the city or the university has managed for over a century. Italy's national register gives girth, height and position and no age at all, so every date here comes from university records, the comune's own pages or local history writing, and where none of those has an answer the page leaves the age blank rather than estimating it. Six of the twelve are cedars or their close relatives, planted as Perugia laid out the public gardens that replaced the papal fortress, which is why the species repeats and the stories do not. The Frontone entry covers two registered holm oaks about seventy metres apart in the same gardens, so its pin is marked approximate: one point cannot honestly stand for both. Four trees here, the two Prepo oaks, the Strada dei Conservoni oak and the Ponte Felcino cypress, are register-only, with no second source and no age. One further register tree is missing on purpose, a holm oak in the cloister of Santa Giuliana, now the Italian Army's language school and not normally open to visitors.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Perugia?
faq.a: By documented date, the Palazzo Murena cedar, planted around 1861. The Frontone holm oaks are probably older, in gardens laid out from 1707, but nobody has dated them.

faq.q: Are Perugia's monumental trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes, all of them. Seven stand on public squares, streets and gardens in the centre, the eighth is in the monumental cemetery, which opens at seven every morning and charges nothing, and the two oaks at Prepo and the downy oak and cypress added since all stand on open roads with no gate.

faq.q: Can I see them all in one walk?
faq.a: Seven of the twelve sit within about a kilometre in the historic centre. The cemetery cedar is a short bus ride out, the two Prepo oaks are three kilometres southwest, and the downy oak and the cypress stand alone about four kilometres out in opposite directions; treat each as its own short trip rather than part of the main walk.

trees.name: The Palazzo Murena Cedar

location.address: Piazza dell'Universita 1 (cloister of Palazzo Murena, Rectorate of the University of Perugia)

trees.story: In 2020 a trumpeter and an accordionist played a concert twelve metres up in this tree. Paolo Fresu and Daniele di Bonaventura performed a set titled Two for Tree from the crown of the Atlas cedar in the cloister of Palazzo Murena, the rectorate of the University of Perugia, with the audience listening from the courtyard below. The tree could take it. It was planted just after Italian unification, around 1861, in the eclectic garden taste of that moment, and is somewhere between 150 and 185 years old depending on which source you ask. The national register gives 485 centimetres of girth and 25 metres of height; La Nazione measured it in 2021 at five metres round, 30 metres tall and 35 metres across the crown. Take either. It is the largest thing inside the cloister by a wide margin, and the walls it grew up between have kept it out of the wind for its whole life. Lightning found it anyway at some point, and left scars still visible on the trunk. Climbing arborists went up in October 2010 to prune it and consolidate the crown, and it was pronounced in excellent health in 2020, the year of the concert. The cloister is free and open during normal building hours, five minutes from Piazza IV Novembre, which makes this the easiest monumental tree in Perugia to reach and the least likely to be spotted from the street.

trees.name: The Atlas Cedar of Piazza Italia
trees.story: This cedar is rooted in the site of a fortress Perugia demolished out of spite. The Rocca Paolina was a papal stronghold built over the houses of the families who opposed the pope, and when the city came out from under papal rule in 1860 it tore the fortress down and laid Piazza Italia over the ground, a square whose entire argument was that the Rocca no longer stood there. The flowerbeds went in with it, and the Atlas cedar in them is one of the survivors of that planting, alongside a red fir of similar age. Local sources call it a century old specimen without fixing a year, so over a century is the honest figure rather than a precise one; the register adds 390 centimetres of girth and 23 metres of height. What makes it worth the two minute walk up from Piazza IV Novembre is where it stands, at the top of Corso Vannucci on the edge of the terrace that looks out over the Umbrian valley. The fortress is still down there under your feet, its lower streets preserved and walkable, which is how most people now arrive at the square, riding escalators up through the ruins of the thing the cedar replaced.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon at Porta Pesa

location.address: Largo di Porta Pesa (Via Brunamonti), Perugia

trees.story: A cedar of Lebanon this thick should be twice as tall. This one measures 410 centimetres round the trunk and 12.5 metres to the top, squat to the point of oddity for the species, and it now carries elastic guy wires and fixed bracing holding its main limbs together. The city installed those over February and March 2025, along with pruning, deadwood removal and a rebalancing of the crown, work done under a care programme run with Umbria's regional forestry service for Perugia's monumental trees. Read cabling as good news. A tree gets braced when somebody has decided it is worth keeping. It grows on the open square at Largo di Porta Pesa, directly in front of the Ciabatti Montessori elementary school, so several generations of Perugian children have had it as the thing outside the window, and the comune calls it century old without naming a year. Cedar of Lebanon reached Italian gardens from the mountains of the Levant, where the surviving old groves are now fenced and counted individually. A low, wide, heavily limbed specimen like this one is what the species does when it grows in the open with nothing competing for light, which is also why it needs the hardware: those limbs are long, horizontal and heavy. Porta Pesa is five to ten minutes on foot from Piazza IV Novembre.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon at Croce Rossa

location.address: Via Masi, Largo della Croce Rossa, Perugia

trees.story: The national register knows how tall this cedar is and not how wide. Its sheet records 18 metres of height and leaves the girth field blank, a gap in the paperwork rather than a lost measurement, and nobody has filled it in since. So the honest description of Perugia's second cedar of Lebanon is this: 18 metres, standing on a public square, and you can judge the trunk yourself when you get there. It grows at Largo della Croce Rossa on Via Masi, a short walk downhill from Piazza Italia and Palazzo Murena, and La Nazione named it specifically in a survey of the city's monumental trees under municipal care, which is how we know it is being looked after rather than merely listed. No age is recorded anywhere. Cedar of Lebanon was planted all over nineteenth century Italy as a status tree, the conifer of the Bible and of Lebanon's flag, which is why a city this size ends up with two of them ten minutes apart and no particular reason for either. Between the pair, this is the taller by a clear margin, 18 metres against the 12.5 of the Porta Pesa cedar, which is roughly what the species does when it has been left to run up rather than out.

trees.name: The Hackberry of Via Fiume
trees.age_estimate: roughly 175 to 300 years, judged from a trunk 4.45 m round
trees.story: Italians call this species spaccasassi, the rock splitter, because its roots get into stone and open it. They plant it in city streets anyway, because little else gives that much shade on that little water. This one has been on Via Fiume long enough to reach 445 centimetres round the trunk and 21 metres tall, a serious size for a hackberry and a very serious size for a tree growing out of a street in a hill town rather than a garden with soil to spare. Perugia's centre is built along a ridge with its streets cut into the slope, so a tree of this age here has spent its whole life finding water under paving. La Nazione named it alongside the city's two cedars of Lebanon in a survey of the monumental trees the comune maintains, and the same programme covers it: inspection, pruning, and the working assumption that it stays. Its age is not on record and no source estimates one. Mediterranean hackberry leafs out late, drops small dark fruit in autumn that the birds clear before most people notice it, and keeps smooth grey bark like a beech into old age, which is the quickest way to tell it from anything else on the street. It is a few minutes' walk from Piazza Italia.

trees.name: The Holm Oaks of Giardini del Frontone

location.address: Giardini del Frontone, Borgo XX Giugno, Perugia

trees.story: On 20 June 1859 papal Swiss Guards and the Antibes Legion came up the hill and sacked Perugia, and these oaks were already old. A local history piece in 2025 put the question directly, asking what the secular holm oaks of the Frontone saw that day, the last serious violence in the city before Italian unification. The gardens are older still. They were laid out from 1707 for the Accademia degli Arcadi, a literary society that wanted somewhere to hold its summer gatherings, on ground used for military drill since the 1400s and, long before that, as an Etruscan necropolis. The avenues of holm oak went in with the garden and were finished through the 1800s, along with the pool, the statues and the Arco del Frontone of 1791. Two of the oaks are individually listed in the national register, at 350 and 342 centimetres round and 15.5 and 21.5 metres tall, standing about 70 metres apart along the same avenues. The pin marks the gardens rather than one trunk, because the walk under the oaks is the thing here, not a single tree. Holm oak holds its leaves all year, so the avenues are dark and cool in August, which is exactly what the Arcadians wanted them for. The gardens are free, opposite the Abbey of San Pietro, fifteen to twenty minutes south of the centro storico on foot.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of the Cimitero Monumentale

location.address: Cimitero Monumentale, Via Enrico dal Pozzo, Perugia

trees.story: Perugia's monumental cemetery opens at seven every morning, costs nothing, and holds a Himalayan cedar with a trunk 496 centimetres round and 23.5 metres of tree above it. Italian monumental cemeteries are built to be walked in. Milan's and Genoa's draw visitors for their sculpture and their planting as much as for the graves, and this one, out on Via Enrico dal Pozzo in the Monteluce district, is the same kind of place: gravel avenues, cypresses, and this cedar over the top of them. The Templar church of San Bevignate, with its thirteenth century frescoes, stands next door. What the tree does not have is a story of its own. No newspaper, history page or municipal notice found so far names it; the register measures it and the comune's page confirms the cemetery and its hours, and that is the whole documentary record, which means its age is unknown rather than approximate. Deodar was a standard cemetery planting across nineteenth century Italy, an evergreen brought down from the Himalaya and chosen for the obvious associations, so a nineteenth century date is likely and unproven. Opening runs to half past five in winter and half past six in summer. It is a twenty minute walk from the centro storico, or a short bus ride.

trees.name: The Cypress of Parco della Cuparella
trees.story: The park this cypress stands in used to be where people dumped things. Perugians called the slope Il Campaccio, roughly the bad field, a steep and disused strip against the medieval walls, and in the 1950s the comune handed it to the Tuscan landscape architect Pietro Porcinai, who turned it into a public garden. The nickname stuck anyway. The Mediterranean cypress here measures 293 centimetres round and 21 metres tall, and it is the closest monumental tree to the centre of Perugia, a couple of hundred metres from Piazza Italia and Piazza dell'Universita, which makes it the one to start or finish a walk on. Cypress is the least surprising tree in Umbria and the most useful. It takes thin, fast draining soil, exactly the conditions on a slope like this one, and its narrow column is the reason Italian hillsides look the way they do in every painting of them. Whether this tree predates Porcinai's redesign or went in as part of it is not recorded, and neither the register nor FAI's heritage listing for the park says. Nobody has published an age. What is on record is the site: free, open, built along the city walls, with the valley below it and the old town directly above.

trees.name: The North Oak of Strada del Gioco
trees.age_estimate: roughly 150 to 300 years, judged from a trunk 4.3 m round
trees.story:
Downy oak is the tree Umbrian hillsides are made of, and hardly any of them get this big. Quercus pubescens takes the dry limestone slopes that better oaks refuse, usually as a modest, crooked, hard-used tree of field edges and scrub. This one is 430 centimetres around and 21 metres tall, which put it on Italy's national monumental register on size alone. It is not even alone: a second oak within eight centimetres of the same girth stands 150 metres down the lane.

Strada del Gioco runs through Prepo, on the slope roughly three kilometres southwest of the walled centre. Perugia's other monumental trees are a nineteenth century story, cedars planted as the city laid out gardens over the ground where the papal fortress had stood. These two are the older landscape showing through: field oaks left where they were while the land around them changed use, which is how a good many large roverelle in central Italy came to survive.

The species is worth knowing in winter. Downy oak is marcescent, tending to hold its dead leaves on the lower branches through the cold months instead of dropping them, so the crown keeps a rustling copper brown long after the rest of the hillside has gone bare.

Italy's register is the only source that names this tree, and it gives a girth, a height and a position and no age, so the numbers here are the register's own and the pin is marked approximate.
trees.how_to_recognise: The northern of the two oaks on Strada del Gioco, about 150 metres up the lane from the other. Size barely separates them: this one is the thicker at 430 centimetres round, and the shorter at 21 metres.

trees.name: The South Oak of Strada del Gioco
trees.age_estimate: roughly 150 to 300 years, judged from a trunk 4.22 m round
trees.story:
The two oaks of Strada del Gioco differ by eight centimetres of girth and one metre of height, and they stand 150 metres apart. This is the thinner and taller of the pair: 422 centimetres around, 22 metres up, and nothing at all on record about its age.

Part of what a downy oak is worth in Umbria is what grows under it. Quercus pubescens is one of central Italy's classic truffle hosts, the fungus forming on oak roots in exactly the limestone soils these trees favour, and a productive oak is a tree with an argument for being left standing when a hillside gets cleared. Whether that is this particular tree's biography, nobody has written down.

Prepo is a working edge of Perugia rather than a monument to it, about three kilometres southwest of the centre and 370 metres up. There is no garden here, no plaque and no gate, just two very large oaks on a lane, which is a different sort of pleasure from the cedars that hold the city's squares. Come in winter for the second one: downy oak hangs onto its dead leaves through the cold months, and a copper crown on a bare slope carries a long way.

Nobody has dated either oak. Italy's register has no age column and no second source names them, so what exists is a girth, a height and a point on a map, and the point is good to within a lane rather than a trunk.
trees.how_to_recognise: The southern of the two oaks on Strada del Gioco, about 150 metres down the lane from the other. Size will not separate them at a glance: this one is fractionally slimmer at 422 centimetres round and fractionally taller at 22 metres.

trees.name: The Downy Oak of Strada dei Conservoni
trees.age_estimate: roughly 150 to 300 years, judged from a trunk 4.27 m round
trees.story:
Four hundred and twenty seven centimetres round is a serious trunk for a species that usually stays modest. Quercus pubescens, downy oak, takes the dry limestone slopes better oaks refuse and grows into a gnarled, workaday tree of field edges rather than a giant, which is exactly why Italy's national register singles this one out.

It stands alone on Strada dei Conservoni, a hillside road climbing to 450 metres, four kilometres from Perugia's walled centre and with no other registered tree anywhere near it. Perugia's other monumental trees mostly belong to a nineteenth century story, cedars planted when the city laid gardens over the ground where the papal fortress once stood. This oak is older news than that. Umbrian hillsides were oak country long before anyone planted an ornamental cedar, and a tree this size on a working lane is the landscape showing through the gardens rather than a garden itself.

Downy oak earns a second look in winter. It is marcescent, holding its dead leaves through the cold months instead of dropping them, so the crown keeps a dry, rust brown rustle on the hillside long after its neighbours have gone bare.

Italy's register is the only document that names this tree. It gives a girth, a height and a point on the map and nothing else, so there is no age here and the pin is marked approximate.

trees.story:
Five metres and forty seven centimetres round is the largest trunk in Perugia's entire national tree register, and it belongs not to one of the city's celebrated garden cedars but to a cypress on a suburban street.

The tree stands on Via Giacomo Puccini in Ponte Felcino, a district that grew up around a Tiber crossing and a railway junction rather than around a palace or a papal fortress, about four kilometres northeast of the historic centre and 200 metres above sea level, low ground for a Perugia register tree. Mediterranean cypress, Cupressus sempervirens, is the tall dark spire of Tuscan and Umbrian cemetery avenues and villa driveways, usually planted in disciplined rows for its shape rather than grown singly to a record size, which makes a single specimen this thick unusual rather than typical of the species.

Nothing in the register says who planted it or when, and no second source names this particular tree, so it carries no age and stands flagged on the strength of one document. What the register does record is a girth that beats every cedar, oak and plane elsewhere on Perugia's list, by a wide margin. Whatever else is unknown about this cypress, its size on the page is not in question.

trees.story:
This cedar's planter is on record, which is rarer than it sounds. Ferdinando Cesaroni, who lived at Villa del Colle del Cardinale from 1892, planted the Cedar of Lebanon in front of the house, beside the oak, together with a rare Japanese cedar. That puts the tree at roughly 130 years old, a figure that comes from the planting rather than a ring count.

The villa had three centuries behind it by then. Cardinal Fulvio della Corgna commissioned it in 1575, in a design attributed to Galeazzo Alessi, and from 1645 the Oddi family reshaped the grounds into an English-style garden. Later the Italian State bought it, and for years it stood abandoned. The gardens reopened on 21 March 2025 after a restoration of about 2 million euros.

The national register lists the cedar at 16.5 metres tall and gives no girth. Photographs of the park show a broad, flat-layered crown spreading low over the lawn, wider than it is high, with Italian cypresses rising behind it. The same register names a deodar, a Monterey cypress and two tall Italian cypresses in the same park, so one ticket covers several old conifers.

The villa is open on weekends and some holidays, and the hours differ between listings. Check before you drive out.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the broad, flat-layered crown spreading low over the lawn, wider than it is tall, with cypresses behind. It stands in front of the villa; the deodar is about 27 metres to its south.

trees.story:
A courtyard in Perugia is named after this tree. The Cortile del Leccio, the courtyard of the holm oak, sits beside the church of Santa Giuliana, and the oak at its centre has a crown about 24 metres across, wider than the tree is tall. The national register measures it at 3.81 metres round and 17.5 metres high.

The monastery around it is far older. Santa Giuliana was founded in 1253 under Pope Innocent IV, a house of Benedictine rule in the Cistercian manner, and its cloister, attributed to Gattapone, was built in 1376 to receive the relics of Saint Giuliana. The oak is younger than the stones but no sapling. The 2025 Monumenti Aperti guide puts it at over 300 years, an event text's figure rather than a ring count, and calls it the green heart of the courtyard.

At its foot stands an old well. It was once filled with rubble and is now closed and raised, and behind the tree a corridor leads to the remains of what is called a Roman road.

The complex belongs to the state and opens at set times rather than every day. It was free on weekends during Monumenti Aperti in September 2025; other listings say visits by reservation two days ahead. Call before you go. It is about a kilometre south of Piazza IV Novembre, some 15 minutes on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the well at its foot, closed and raised, and a crown about 24 metres across. It stands alone in the Cortile del Leccio, the courtyard beside the church of Santa Giuliana named after it.

trees.story:
Of all the old trees at Villa del Colle del Cardinale that Italy's register has put a tape round, this Himalayan cedar has the thickest trunk. The national register gives it 4.28 metres round and 20 metres tall, at about 300 metres above sea level on the hills north-west of Perugia.

Who planted it is a fair question with no firm answer. Ferdinando Cesaroni, who lived at the villa from 1892, is recorded as planting exotic conifers in front of the house, and the sources name a Cedar of Lebanon and a Japanese cedar among them. They do not name this deodar, so its date stays open. If you know when it went in, tell us.

The house it stands before goes back to 1575, when Cardinal Fulvio della Corgna commissioned it in a design attributed to Galeazzo Alessi. The Oddi family turned the grounds into an English-style garden from 1645. Much later the Italian State bought the villa, left it empty for years, and then spent about 2 million euros restoring the gardens, which reopened on 21 March 2025.

The deodar stands about 27 metres south of the villa's Cedar of Lebanon, and a Monterey cypress grows some 35 metres to its west, so the three make a short circuit of one lawn. The park opens on weekends for a small fee; check the hours before you drive out.

trees.story:
A Monterey cypress is an uncommon tree in Umbria, and this one is big enough to make Italy's national register. It measures 3.61 metres round and 18.5 metres tall, a broad, dense, dark shape that reads quite differently from the slim Italian cypresses in the same park, which rise to 28 and 29 metres as the tallest trees here.

It stands on the lawn of Villa del Colle del Cardinale, the country house Cardinal Fulvio della Corgna commissioned in 1575 on the hills north-west of Perugia, in a design attributed to Galeazzo Alessi. From 1645 the Oddi family reshaped the grounds as an English-style garden. Ferdinando Cesaroni, resident from 1892, planted exotic conifers in front of the house, but the sources name only a Cedar of Lebanon and a Japanese cedar, so they do not tell us whether this cypress was his. Nobody has published its age. If you know, tell us.

The villa later passed to the Italian State, stood abandoned for years, and reopened on 21 March 2025 after a restoration of the gardens costing about 2 million euros. Visit the cypress with its neighbours, the Himalayan cedar about 35 metres to the east and the Cedar of Lebanon about 50 metres to the north-east. The park opens on weekends for a small fee, and the listed hours disagree, so check before going.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its broad, dense, dark crown, much wider and shorter than the park's slim Italian cypresses. It stands about 35 metres west of the Himalayan cedar and 50 metres south-west of the Cedar of Lebanon.
